title: Zombies serve cocktails and Pochita turns into parfait at Universal Studios Japan this Halloween
description: Are you ready for a taste of terror? As Universal Studios Japan marks its 25th anniversary, the park is bursting with thrills with its milestone 15th edition of Halloween Horror Nights. Running from September 11 to November 8, this year’s event pairs the classic street scares with an array of spook-filled food and drink offerings […]
content:
Are you ready for a taste of terror?

As Universal Studios Japan marks its 25th anniversary, the park is bursting with thrills with its milestone 15th edition of Halloween Horror Nights. Running from September 11 to November 8, this year’s event pairs the classic street scares with an array of spook-filled food and drink offerings that make it well worth a visit.

The headliner for 2026’s new additions is the park’s first-ever Zombie Bar. Occupying Wharf Cafe in the San Francisco area of the park and operating nightly from 6:00 p.m., it features zombified crew members serving eerie signature drinks themed around past park monsters. Highlights include a strawberry-milk Cutie Zombie drink, a non-alcoholic lychee sour for circus zombie fans, and a blood orange and lemon sour inspired by chainsaw zombies.

▼ Cutie Zombie’s Sweet Temptation — Strawberry Milk

▼ Circus Zombie’s Madness: Lychee Non-Alcoholic Sour

▼ Chainsaw Zombie’s Rampage — Blood Orange & Lemon Sour

Over at Universal Market, high school zombies take the center stage with a creepy school festival theme. Visitors can enjoy blackcurrant waffles from the Zombie Cheerleading Club, garlic-oil experimental takoyaki from the Science Club, or a cheese and onion kalbi (Korean marinated beef ribs) rice dog designed by the ravenous American Football Club, with a night-exclusive banana ice cream to indulge in for dessert.

▼ #Deco Champion Zombie Cheer Squad Cassis Waffle

▼ Burst! Zombie Science Club Experimental Takoyaki — with Umami Garlic Oil

▼ Muscle Rampage! Zombie American Football Club’s Cheese Beef Kalbi Rice Sandwich

▼ Zombie Banana Ice — Does a Banana Count as a Snack?

Anime and gaming enthusiasts have a ton to look forward to as well, thanks to collaborations with Resident Evil and Chainsaw Man. Coinciding with the 30th anniversary of Resident Evil, known as “Biohazard” in Japan, a croissant sandwich filled with chicken, vegetables, and a green-herb basil sauce is offered to honor the new Resident Evil Requiem: The Dive maze, along with a bitter chocolate churro to pay homage to agent Leon S. Kennedy, both being sold at the food cart in front of Space Fantasy – The Ride and accompanied by some original merchandise.

▼ Green Herb Recovery Croissant Bun — Basil Sauce & Chicken and Leon S. Kennedy’s Dark Chocolate Churritos

Chainsaw Man fans should swing by the food cart near Cinema 4-D to pick up a keema curry Chainsaw Man Bun, expressing the transformed Denji, alongside an orange-vanilla Pochita frozen parfait, with Pochita’s posterior on full display as he digs into the dessert. Additionally, a full lineup of original goods will be unveiled in the Cinema 4-D store, such as T-shirts featuring Chainsaw Man fighting the Halloween Horror Nights Devil, and cute keychains of Pochita in a mummy costume.

▼ Chainsaw Bun with Keema Curry Filling and Pochita’s Frozen Parfait ― Orange & Vanilla

Original design coasters feature cover photos of songs used in past Zombie de Dance performances, as well as popular zombies that have made countless guests scream until now, but only one will be handed out at random for every single set menu order. Sink your teeth into a burger full of horror vibes with scarlet sauce dripping from pitch-black buns at Mel’s Drive-In, or a pizza drizzled with sinister black mayonnaise sauce from Louie’s N.Y. Pizza Parlor to start your zombie coaster collection.

▼ Warning! Macaroni and Cheese Burger: Horror Nights 15th Anniversary Meal with Coaster and Caution! Cajun Chicken Pizza: Horror Nights 15th Anniversary Meal with Coaster

Whether you are sipping on an unholy cocktail served by an undead crew member, grabbing a collectible coaster, or digging into a parfait featuring a dog’s buttocks after surviving a haunted maze, this year’s limited-run lineup of food embraces the terrifying nature of the Halloween season for an immersion-packed reason to stay in the park long after the sunset.

title: Trial of terminally ill cancer patient who found 22 million yen on the street and kept it ends
description: Defendant described money as a “gift from God.” They say truth is stranger than fiction, but sometimes truth is exactly as strange as fiction. Such was the case of a 43-year-old man who, shortly after having the worst day of his life, suddenly had the best day of his life in a twist of fate […]
content:
Defendant described money as a “gift from God.”

They say truth is stranger than fiction, but sometimes truth is exactly as strange as fiction. Such was the case of a 43-year-old man who, shortly after having the worst day of his life, suddenly had the best day of his life in a twist of fate that might even be considered cliché if seen in a movie.

Earlier this year, the man, who lives in the city of Higashimatsushima, Miyagi Prefecture, was told that his cancer that had gone into remission was recurring, and he only had two or three months to live. He later described feeling as if he had given up on everything at that point and just wandered around aimlessly.

Not too long after that, at about noon on 5 March, a security crew was transporting the cash from a game center in the nearby city of Sendai. As they were loading it into an armored car, one of the guards dropped a bag, and they drove off without noticing it. Just then, the terminally ill man happened to be walking by and saw the satchel lying on the sidewalk.

▼ The area where the bag was found is rather busy.

He passed it at first, but curiosity got the better of him. He turned around, picked it up, and took it to a public restroom, where he pried it open with a craft knife to find 22 million yen (US$139,000) in cash. He said that at the time, he thought it “was a gift from God,” and for the next four and a half months, spent 18 million yen ($114,000) of the money on medical treatments and traveling abroad.

Naturally, the parties involved in losing the 22 million yen were determined to get it back. With the help of police, they eventually caught up with the man and arrested him for misappropriation of lost property in July.

On 19 October, his trial was held and lasted only one day, with the man admitting to the charges against him. In closing arguments, the prosecution described the man’s actions as “utterly selfish” and requested a one-year prison sentence, while the defense said that due to the man’s mental state at the time, a suspended sentence would be appropriate.

Sentencing is scheduled for 6 November, but the court of public opinion seems split on the matter of whether the man’s actions were excusable given his situation or a crime that deserves justice despite it.

“It wasn’t a gift from God. It was lost property, and he stole it.”
“I’d probably have done the same thing. It’s like something out of a manga.”
“It was the guards who lost the money. Can a judge really expect him to use sound judgment just after being told he was going to die?”
“He should have just turned it in. They probably would have given him a reward, and he could have enjoyed that guilt-free.”
“If I drop money on the street and someone takes it. I blame myself.”
“Is he even going to survive this trial?”
“I wonder if using the money on medical treatment helped.”
“Maybe the next gift from God will be a miracle cure. Then, he’ll have to work the rest of his life paying that money off.”

The firm in charge of transporting the money had the 22 million yen covered by insurance, and the man has already entered into an agreement with the insurance company to repay the money. According to the terms he must pay them 30,000 yen ($190) a month until the full amount is paid, which should take until sometime around the year 2076.

title: Japanese scientists developing cute, autonomously swarming robo dogs for anti-bear patrols [Video]
description: Hacchan is a mecha version of an Akita Inu hunting dog. Along with a bit of chilly autumn crispiness, there’s also some apprehension in the air in Japan. That’s because we’re getting to the part of the year when bears start bulking up in preparation of hibernating, which means they’ll be growing bolder and roaming […]
content:
Hacchan is a mecha version of an Akita Inu hunting dog.

Along with a bit of chilly autumn crispiness, there’s also some apprehension in the air in Japan. That’s because we’re getting to the part of the year when bears start bulking up in preparation of hibernating, which means they’ll be growing bolder and roaming wider in their search for stuff to eat,

With bear attacks having become a topic of heightened concern in recent years, and northern Japan having the country’s largest bear populations, earlier this year Akita Prefectural University began accepting proposals from faculty and students for its Bear-Tech Solution Contest. A total of 41 entries were submitted, and on October 13 a selection of the most promising ideas were presented in Akita City, including an idea for a surprisingly cute anti-bear robot dog.

Called Hacchan, the robot named after Japan’s most famous Akita Inu, Hachiko. Rather than hang out around Shibuya Station waiting for its master to come home and munching on grilled chicken handouts, though, Hacchan’s behavior is inspired by the Akita Inu hunting dogs that would accompany Akita Prefecture’s traditional huntsmen into the woods in days of yore.

▼ Hacchan can be seen at the point in the video queued here.

However, unlike actual hunting dogs, Hacchan has been created with a nonviolent outcome in mind. The quadrupedal robot is meant for deployment on the edge of farms or towns, and when its camera detects a bear, it uses an internal speaker to play the sound of a dog barking loudly in order to scare the animal off and make it retreat back into the woods. By sharing its location data, Hacchan can even call other units to the scene, creating a pack of robo dogs for a more intimidating presence, while also building a database of bear sighting and behavior to help the robots efficiently and autonomously patrol the outer edges of the community.

Researcher Masayuki Yoshida of the university’s Regional Collaboration and Research Promotion Center, who’s leading the development of Hacchan, says they hope to begin field testing the robot dogs before the end of the year.

Ministop is usually the Japanese convenience store chain that people equate with fresh soft serve ice cream, but that may be about to change now that one of The Big Three chains, Family Mart, seems to be experimenting with soft serve at four locations in Tokyo. Strangely, however, we couldn’t find any official press release related to it on Family Mart’s website, and October seems like an odd time to unveil a frozen dessert. Perhaps the mystery is meant to be part of the allure…

Our very own zany reporter and sweets enthusiast Mr. Sato had gotten a hot tip that the Kanda Awaji-cho location is one of the stores offering soft serve. He headed over to check it out for himself and found an unassuming poster out front, but that was about it. He would have thought they would be making a bigger fuss of it.

The three flavors being offered are milk, matcha, and mix (milk & matcha). Each one is offered in a “short size” (250 yen/US$1.60) or “giga size” (298 yen) and can be ordered in a cup or cone.

▼ The giga size is pictured most prominently below, while the short size is pictured in milk flavor-form in the bottom left.

Orders for the soft serve should be placed at the counter, and there are handy ordering cards with each of the three flavors for you to hand over to the staff. Be sure to specify if you’d like a short size, as giga seems to be the default.

Mr. Sato of course sprung for the giga size, and it was ready quite quickly. Here was his first-ever Family Mart soft serve cone!

It started melting right away so he quickly snapped a couple of photos and dug in. It was a rich, creamy milk flavor with moderate sweetness and the perfect full-bodied texture inside his mouth.

He had the feeling that Ministop’s milky flavor is a bit more prominent, though he can’t confirm that without trying them side by side.

▼ Regardless, he’ll scream for ice cream no matter what!

Rumors are that Family Mart hopes to sell the soft serve at four more stores in the Tokyo area by the end of the year as well, bringing the total to eight stores. Mr. Sato is happy as long as there’s an increasing number of opportunities to find convenience store soft serve moving forward–and he’ll keep supporting Ministop, too!

content:
The Straw Hat Pirates sail into the City of Angels with cool California-exclusive merch.

The hearts of otaku were dealt a painful blow this week when visa problems lead to the sudden cancellation of two Umamusume concerts in Los Angeles, which were supposed to be the franchise’s first musical performances on American soil. It’s not all bad news for anime fans in the City of Angels, though, as the opening date has been announced for the first-ever permanent One Piece specialty store in the U.S.!

It’s not going to be stuck in the back corner of some random strip mall, either. The One Piece Mugiwara Store will be waiting for visitors inside downtown Los Angeles’ Westfield Century City shopping mall on Santa Monica Boulevard, right down the street from Beverly Hills.

▼ Mugiwara is the Japanese word for “straw,” as in “Straw Hat Pirates”

The shop will be opening on November 6, stocked with a wide variety of One Piece merch, featuring both items imported from Japan and exclusive items that aren’t available anywhere else, even at the One Piece Mugiwara Store branches in Japan, such as apparel items with a California license plate motif, surfer-version Chopper, or the message “I love LA” with an Op-Op Fruit in place of a heart.

The Surfer Chopper design was created specially for the L.A. store, and will also feature in some sort of interactive in-store experience that includes audio messages for visitors to hear.

View this post on Instagram

▼ Figure,s furoshiki wrapping cloths, and a whole lot of blind-buy trinkets will be among the items imported from Japan.

With the One Piece anime debuting 27 years ago, and the manga two years before that, there should be plenty of pent-up demand among American fans for an entire shop dedicated to the series, and as a crowd control measure, reservations will be necessary to enter the One Piece Mugiwara Store between November 6 and 12, and can be made through the shop’s official website here.

title: Pokémon Company announces first-ever permanent Pokémon store to open outside Asia
description: After decades of delighting fans in Asia, Pokémon store heads to a new continent. It’s impossible to overstate how much of a pop cultural institution Pokémon is in Japan. Between the anime, video games, cards, and mountains of plushies, Pokémon has been sparking the imaginations and warming the hearts of multiple generations of fans, and […]
content:
After decades of delighting fans in Asia, Pokémon store heads to a new continent.

It’s impossible to overstate how much of a pop cultural institution Pokémon is in Japan. Between the anime, video games, cards, and mountains of plushies, Pokémon has been sparking the imaginations and warming the hearts of multiple generations of fans, and if any of them are looking for some cool new merch, they can pop into any of the roughly two dozen Pokémon specialty stores Japan has, stretching from Hokkaido in the north to Okinawa in the south.

But the franchise has grown into a massive success overseas as well, and the Pokémon Company has announced that it will finally be opening the first-ever permanent Pokémon store outside of Asia, and London is the lucky city that’s receiving the honor.

In Japan, Pokémon specialty stores come in three types: Pokémon Center megastores, moderately sized Pokémon Stores, and compact Pokémon Center Satellites. It’s not clear which, if any, of those classes the London store will fall into, but the official announcement says it will be a “Pokémon retail destination” and “the ultimate destination for Pokémon fans and include a variety of exclusive merchandise and one-of-a-kind experiences for Trainers of all ages,” so the plan is clearly for something much grander in scale and ambition than a glorified souvenir stand.

This will make the U.K. the fourth country with a permanent Pokémon. store, with the other non-Japan shops being in Taiwan (Taipei) and Singapore. In addition to the London location, the Pokémon Company says it’s also planning to launch “several” other branches outside Asia.

Unfortunately, the London Pokémon store isn’t scheduled to open until 2029, but that again speaks to the likelihood that it’s probably going to be a large-scale project, and if there’s anyone worth waiting for, it’s Pikachu, right?

title: Japanese sushi etiquette: You may have been ordering sushi wrong this whole time
description: Read this before ordering fatty tuna at a sushi restaurant in Japan. There are a lot of ways to enjoy sushi in Japan, but if you want to earn brownie points (or should we say sushi points?) and impress those around you, you might want to hold back on your favourites and follow a rule […]
content:
Read this before ordering fatty tuna at a sushi restaurant in Japan.

There are a lot of ways to enjoy sushi in Japan, but if you want to earn brownie points (or should we say sushi points?) and impress those around you, you might want to hold back on your favourites and follow a rule of thumb that few tourists know about.

It’s a traditional approach that makes a lot of sense, but it might require some discipline, as it involves starting with lighter fish before moving on to fattier, richer varieties. That means holding back on some of the more popular crowd-pleasers like fatty tuna, and starting with varieties like flounder, sea bream and other delicately flavoured fish.

▼ Scallops are another good choice.

This sushi protocol actually became a topic of debate online recently, when a 30-year-old Japanese office worker went to dinner with the president of his new company and was reprimanded after requesting fatty tuna at the start of the meal. He was loudly scolded by the president, who told him that his choice was inconsiderate, and he should know basic sushi etiquette as a working adult.

The president insisted that diners should always start with white fish, like flounder. When the young office worker explained that he wasn’t fond of white fish, the president criticised him for claiming to like sushi at all. Needless to say, the incident left the worker questioning whether he’d made the right decision in joining the company.

▼ Look boss, I wanted to like you, but I don’t love you like fatty tuna.

While it does sound like the president could’ve been less scathing in his remarks, he actually was referring to a recognised approach to eating sushi. Sushi enthusiasts often recommend starting with delicate white fish, such as flounder or sea bream, as their subtle flavours would be harder to appreciate after eating stronger-flavoured fish and richer cuts like fatty tuna. In fact, when sushi chefs serve “omakase” set meals to diners, they often follow this rule of thumb, as moving from lighter to richer flavours helps diners enjoy the differences between each type of sushi.

Rather than being an absolute rule, though, this progression from light to rich is a general guideline, and a lot of diners these days will simply eat whatever they want whenever they want, especially when dining out at a conveyor belt sushi chain restaurant, where people aren’t really watching what you do.

▼ Heck, you could even order beef short ribs if you wanted to, but on the Sushi Bus, anything goes.

Image©SoraNews24

Like all dining choices, the decision on what to eat, and when, is ultimately up to the diner. So if you’re eating at a sushi counter, with the chef right in front of you, ordering white fish before richer varieties will let them know that you have respect for proper sushi etiquette. If you’re more cavalier, you can take your chances and simply order fatty fish… and hope that the person next to you isn’t a company president with a stickler for the rules, or else you’ll be schooled.

title: New Studio Ghibli anime gets extended run at the only cinema in Japan where it’s being shown
description: If you’re planning a trip to Japan soon, you’ll have a better chance of seeing A Night in the Valley of Witches. Studio Ghibli is world-famous for its feature-length anime movies, but what a lot of fans don’t know is that the studio has a roster of animated shorts that are just as captivating. These […]
content:
If you’re planning a trip to Japan soon, you’ll have a better chance of seeing A Night in the Valley of Witches.

Studio Ghibli is world-famous for its feature-length anime movies, but what a lot of fans don’t know is that the studio has a roster of animated shorts that are just as captivating. These rare beauties are like hidden gems for Ghibli hunters, as they’re screened at just two places in the world — the Ghibli Museum in Tokyo and Ghibli Park in Aichi Prefecture. Making them even more of a rarity is the fact that the museum and park screen the shorts one at a time, with the line-up usually changing monthly.

▼ My Neighbour Totoro sequel Mei and the Kittenbus is one such short film.

Now, though, Ghibli Park is making an exception to the rule, by extending the screening period for the studio’s newest short, A Night in the Valley of Witches, which debuted at Cinema Orion inside Ghibli’s Grand Warehouse in July. The movie has been so well-received that the park now says it’s decided to extend the run right through to June 2027, giving fans more time to view this newest Ghibli gem.

Although this particular film is exclusive to Ghibli Park, there really is no better place in the world to see it, as the storyline is set in the park’s own Valley of Witches area.

▼ The area honours Ghibli’s witchy characters with buildings like the bakery from Kiki’s Delivery Service.

According to the synopsis, A Night in the Valley of Witches follows the story of a new recruit at the park, who receives a surprising number of requests to repair numerous buildings on the grounds. While carrying out the repairs, a number of odd things occur – a fireplace comes alight on its own and water gushes spontaneously from the taps.

Though he’s shaken by what’s going on, one of his senior colleagues, Kikue, dismisses his concerns, until one night at midnight, after the park closes, he heads to the Valley of Witches, where he finds Kikue clad in a cape. Kikue reveals herself to be a witch and then chants a spell, setting the stage for some mysterious magic…

With Valley of the Witches being a real-life area of the park, watching the film in this setting is a real treat for fans, especially at Halloween, when there will be a special after-dark outdoor screening of the film within the area. Outside of the special Halloween event, which is a children-only affair, the screening will take place at Cinema Orion, which isn’t too far from the Valley of Witches, so you’ll still be immersed in the world of Ghibli while you watch it.

The extended run is welcome news for Ghibli fans, because the additional time gives visitors more chance of catching the film while planning their trips. Ghibli Park tickets must be booked in advance, with reservations generally opening at 2 p.m. on the 10th of each month for visits two months later. Tickets are still expected to be in high demand, though, so you’ll want to book early to make sure you don’t miss the run, although our fingers are firmly crossed that they might consider extending it even further, to give even more fans the chance to see it.

title: Police in Japan likely to gain authority to hack phones to check messaging apps
description: Regulations would be similar to those for phone taps. The Japanese cabinet has approved a bill that would grant expanded remote analysis powers to investigators. “Remote analysis” might sound like the police will be getting better long-distance camera lenses, or maybe using some sort of new IT system to get lab work done without having […]
content:
Regulations would be similar to those for phone taps.

The Japanese cabinet has approved a bill that would grant expanded remote analysis powers to investigators. “Remote analysis” might sound like the police will be getting better long-distance camera lenses, or maybe using some sort of new IT system to get lab work done without having to transport physical evidence to/from an outside facility, but this regulatory amendment is specifically for allowing the police to analyze electronic devices used for messaging apps without being in possession of the device itself.

In other words, the bill is to allow the Japanese police to hack people’s phones.

Proponents of the amendment say such expanded powers are necessary in order to combat the rapidly increasing activities of criminal groups known as tokuryu. Formed from the words tokumei (anonymous) and ryudo (fluid), tokuryu groups operate with ringleaders recruiting participants for criminal acts via encrypted messaging apps. Instead of a regular crew of accomplices, ringleaders often employ members on a one-time basis, treating criminal activities like gig-based part-time jobs. The lack of in-person meetings makes traditional preventive surveillance by the police, such as stakeouts or tapped phone lines, virtually useless in acquiring usable information, and even when the individuals who directly carried out a crime are caught, it’s difficult for questioning to lead investigators back to the ringleaders, as those recruited to do the job may not themselves known who their illicit employer is.

So on October 16, the Cabinet approved a bill to allow the police to remotely hack phones and examine encrypted messaging app data they suspect is being used to plan a crime. This isn’t carte blanche to go looking through anyone’s phones they want, though. Much like with wiretaps, the bill requires investigators to obtain a warrant from a judge prior to conducting the hack. Acquisition of a warrant would be dependent on factors such as urgency and difficulty of obtaining the information through alternate methods, and warrants would only be issued for crimes of suitable seriousness, such as robbery or fraud, and only specially skilled investigators designated by the National Police Agency’s commissioner general would be authorized to perform the hacks.

By utilizing these expanded powers, investigators hope to be able to obtain information such as the names and addresses of tokuryu members planning crimes, as well as information regarding specific methodology, such as weapons to be used, and identify victims, all of which they believe can be used to stop the crimes before they occur. Data deemed to be irrelevant to criminal activity will not be retained by the police, according to the structure of the bill.

Following the bill’s approval by the Cabinet on October 16, it has been introduced to the current parliamentary session of the Japanese diet, where it is expected to be approved and go into effect sometime within the next six months.

content:
Slowpoke will naturally, though, be arriving a little later than Pikachu and Diglett.

It’s become a yearly tradition for Mister Donut, Japan’s favorite donut chain, to bake up batches of Pokémon donuts as we get into the back half of autumn.

Every year sees the return of the Pikachu donut, because you can’t have a Poké-party and not invite the face of the franchise. So with Mister Donut having just announced its Pokémon lineup for 2026, one of the treats is, naturally, the Fluffy Pikachu donut, filled with whipped cream and covered in custard-flavored chocolate flakes. This year, for the first time ever, the donut’s rosy cheeks are rendered with a pair of chewy strawberry gummies.

But Pikachu never shows up to Mister Donut alone, as the chain always has at least one other Pocket Monster species represented in its collaboration lineup. So on the same day as fans can start munching on the Fluffy Pikachu, they can also chow down on the Pon de Alolan Diglett.

The Pon de Alolan Diglett is a crossover within a crossover, placing a Diglett inside one of Mister Donut’s flagship Pon de Ring donuts (made up of a ring of eight balls of dough) so that the semi-subterranean-situated Pokémon looks like it’s bursting forth from the earth, with a sprinkling of crunchy chocolate bits playing the part of rocks and rubble. Unlike the Diglett donut from 2024, this one is an Alolan version, differentiated by the tuft on top of its head, and the coatings of caramel and chocolate, plus the Diglett’s custard cream filling, give you a variety of rich flavors to enjoy.

Both the Pikachu and Diglett donuts go on sale via pre-orders (via the Mister Donut website or app) on October 27, with in-store pickup dates from November 2 followed by walk-in availability on November 4. There’s also one more Pokémon donut in the works, but it won’t be going on sale until a few later. That lackadaisical attitude is totally appropriate, though, because it’s a Slowpoke donut!

▼ “Let’s take it nice and slow,” says the Slowpoke donut announcement.

Yes, Slowpoke, whose bragging rights include holding the highest political office of any Pokémon species, is adding to its resume by making its Mister Donut debut. The Slowpoke Donut is a creampuff-like confectionary with a white chocolate coating, dusting of strawberry milk sugar, whipped cream ears, and chocolate eyes and nose. Preorders for it can be made from November 18 for pickup dates starting November 23, and walk-in sales start November 25.

And for fans who want to look at Pokémon, but not necessarily eat them, there’s the Pokémon Assemble donut, a soft, angel food cake-like donut with a chocolate coating, whipped and custard creams inside, and four different adorable Pokémon illustration designs for its wrapper, which goes on sale at the same time as the Pikachu and Diglett donuts.

The Pikachu and Slowpoke donuts are priced at 345 yen (US$2.20) for takeout or 352 yen for eat-in, while the Alolan Diglelt is 367/374 yen and the Pokémon Assemble 237/242 yen. If you’re willing to shell out a little extra, though, there are also two different Pokémon donut/merch bundles. The 2,200-yen “Goods Set” includes your choice of any two of the Pikachu, Diglett, and Pokémon Assemble donuts, plus one Pon de Wreath (another Pon de Ring variation, this one with sprinkles and either caramel or white chocolate coating), and your choice of one of two Pokémon blanket patterns.

▼ The blankets measure 100 x 82 centimeters (39.4 x 32.3 inches)

There’s also a 1,180-yen “Kids’ Goods Set,” with one Pokémon donut, one Pon de Wreath, and a child-size drinking glass. Both sets can be preordered starting October 27, with pickup dates from November 2.

Finally, Mister Donut will have Pokémon-illustration takeout boxes overlapping with the availability of the Pokémon donuts, while supplies last.

Similarly, the donuts themselves will be available for a limited, but unspecified, time while supplies last, so, as always, the wise thing to do is to eat dessert as soon as possible.

title: It’s time for the kokia to shine at this herb gardens and ropeway attraction in Kobe
description: The park’s Garden Fest 2026 -Autumn- event is enveloped in a sea of fire this year that’s perfect for making fall memories. ’Tis the season for kochia (bassia scoparia), nicknamed kokia in Japanese and firebush in English, to have their moment in the spotlight. content:
The park’s Garden Fest 2026 -Autumn- event is enveloped in a sea of fire this year that’s perfect for making fall memories.

’Tis the season for kochia (bassia scoparia), nicknamed kokia in Japanese and firebush in English, to have their moment in the spotlight. Mt. Hakodate’s Kokia Park in Shiga Prefecture and Hitachi Seaside Park in Ibaraki are two of the most famous places for viewing kokia in all of their crimson, autumn glory, but this year, a locale in Kobe promises to raise a colorful challenge.

Situated at an elevation of 400 meters (1,434 feet), Kobe Nunobiki Herb Gardens & Ropeway’s Garden Fest 2026 -Autumn- event from September 12 through December 6 is well underway, but now through the end of October is the peak time to see the kokia looking like they’re on fire. The grounds have three main areas where kokia have been incorporated into the landscaping, including the following spot right outside of the park’s Glass House where they take center stage.

▼ Flames of crimson

It’s a perfect spot to take a photo looking like you’re engulfed in flames.

The second spot is the Windy Hill Lawn Plaza, a windswept spot on slightly higher grounds with Kobe’s modern cityscape in the background.

Here, you can recline in hammocks while admiring the contrast of vivid red and skyscraper silver.

While lounging, enjoy lazily watching the gondolas pass by on the ropeway as well.

The third spot is by one of the flower and herb gardens where the kokia mingle with their other fall cousins like the silver cock’s comb pictured below.

▼ Kokia with orange zinnias

The gardens are home to approximately 200 kinds of plants and 75,000 individual herbs and flowers, so your eyes will never tire of the different color combinations.

The Kobe Nunobiki Herb Gardens & Ropeway is currently following its fall season hours through November 6, which are from 10 a.m.-5 p.m. (last entry at 4:30 p.m.) on weekdays and 10 a.m.-8:30 p.m. (last entry at 5 p.m.) on weekends. The ropeway opens at 9:30 a.m. and the last ride down is at 5:15 p.m. on weekdays and 9 p.m. on weekends. A standard entrance fee for one adult with a round-trip ropeway ticket and entrance to the Herb Garden is 2,500 yen for adults (US$16) and 1,250 yen for children (elementary through junior high school), though there are some discounts for those entering after 5 p.m. who wish to view the gardens only.

For some gastronomic fun while you’re in Kobe, consider stopping by this retro eatery specializing in sobameshi that we recently enjoyed.

title: Umamusume anime concerts unable to obtain visas from U.S. government, cancel L.A. shows
description: Horse girls get stuck in the starting gate ahead of what would have been the franchise’s first-ever concerts in America. October 22 and 23 were supposed to be big days for the Umamusume franchise. Coming roughly a year and a half since the launch of the Umamusume: Pretty Derby mobile game, concerts featuring the franchise’s […]
content:
Horse girls get stuck in the starting gate ahead of what would have been the franchise’s first-ever concerts in America.

October 22 and 23 were supposed to be big days for the Umamusume franchise. Coming roughly a year and a half since the launch of the Umamusume: Pretty Derby mobile game, concerts featuring the franchise’s vocal cast were planned for back-to-back days at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, marking the first-ever Umamusume concerts in America.

Unfortunately, while the venue, costuming, and choreography were all ostensibly good to go, visas to enter the U.S. were not, and both concerts have now been cancelled, just days before they were scheduled to take place.

As we previously reported, on the night of October 18 (Los Angeles time), the official Umamusume website and social media channels made the sudden announcement that the concerts were in jeopardy as a result of the necessary visas still not having been approved, despite organizers “working with lawyers and promoters in the U.S. to secure the visas necessary to enter the US since over six months ago.” With time running out to travel to Los Angeles and carry out on-site prep work, the organizers said a decision would need to be made by the following night, and the one they’ve made is to cancel the shows, announcing:

“It is with heavy hearts that we must announce the cancellation of the Umamusume: Pretty Derby–7th Event: The Stage in Los Angeles concerts planned for Oct 22–23, 2026. Although we have coordinated repeatedly with all parties concerned and explored every possible option in our efforts to make this event happen, we were unable to obtain the necessary visas for entry into the US, so we have come to the painful conclusion that holding the concerts is no longer possible.”

The statement goes on to “sincerely apologize for the inconvenience and concern this causes, and for announcing this so close to the event date,” and that last part makes this an especially aggravating turn of events. The two Los Angeles dates were the only scheduled stops in the U.S. for the Umamusume world tour, so there are definitely fans who made travel reservations in order to see the shows. Even though the cancellation statement says that refunds will be issued for tickets that were purchased (either to see the concerts in-person or to watch the planned live-streams), recouping the costs of things like airline, hotels, and rental car reservations is going to be something fans are going to have to do on their own, and full refunds for those are probably going to be hard to come by on such short notice. There’s also the fact that, with the concerts having been scheduled for Thursday and Friday, many fans also likely took time off from work in order to attend the now-cancelled event.

The organizers do seem sympathetic to the fact that Trainers (as Umamusume fans are called within the fandom) may have grievances greater than just the cost of their concert tickets, and the statement says “[We are] looking into possible responses to Trainers who were planning to attend the concert in person. This will take some time, so we ask for your patience.”

As for where the blame lies, it’s hard to say without more details, and that information probably won’t be publicly disclosed. It’s generally pretty easy for Japanese nationals to obtain visas to enter the U.S. as tourists. They do have to complete the U.S. government’s ESTA (Electronic System for Travel Authorization) form and pay a fee, but those can be done entirely online and the process can be completed in just a few days’ time.

The U.S. government has never been known for speediness in processing work/professional activity visas, though, and needing more than six months for everything to be finalized wouldn’t be a record for complex or sensitive projects. The number of visas the concert organizers needed to obtain could also have been a complicating factor. 17 voice actresses were slated to take the stage, and they’d be traveling with administrative and support staff too. It hasn’t been disclosed if none of the potentially dozens of visa applications were approved in time, or if the concert cancellations are a result of certain key visas not being ready. It’s also worth noting that the organizers haven’t explicitly stated that the visa applications were rejected, so it’s possible that they’re still pending, but no longer had any chance of being ready in time to travel/prepare for the concerts.

On the other hand, while Umamusume rights-holder Cygames, Inc. is listed as the concerts’ organizer, production is credited to Bandai Namco Music Live Inc., a division of Bandai Namco, the biggest anime promoter/merchandiser in the industry. Sending talent overseas for promotional appearances isn’t something Bandai Namco is just now trying out for the first time, so you’d expect them to apply their experience and start the necessary visa applications with ample time to be approved, which suggests that the process was egregiously slow for the Umamusume concerts.

The next scheduled city on the Umamusume world tour is London, followed by Seoul, and then a return to Japan for a finale in Yokohama. None of those concerts have announced dates or venues yet, though, so it’s possible that replacement concerts could be organized for the U.S., but the chain of events that lead to the cancellation of the L.A. shows suggests that they wouldn’t be possible until, at the very least, more than six months from now.

title: Flying Mud Boat teahouse is a hidden gem in Japan that boggles the mind

content:
This site takes traditional architecture to new heights, like a Ghibli world come to life.

We’re always on the hunt for hidden gems and little-known sights in Japan, so when we heard about a teahouse that was suspended in the air, we immediately sent our reporter Natsuno Futon over to Nagano Prefecture to check it out.

Called the “Flying Mud Boat”, the unusual structure is tucked away in Chino City, on a plot of land that houses two other equally charming teahouses. The setting is so whimsical that it feels like a Ghibli world come to life, with calming hues and natural materials helping the buildings blend into the surrounding greenery.

▼  The first sight to greet you is a boat-like object that literally hangs in the air.

This is Sora Tobu Dorobune, which translates as Flying Mud Boat, and it was designed by architect Terunobu Fujimori.

Ever since his student days, Fujimori had always wanted to build something that floated in midair, and he finally got the chance to bring the idea to life when he created the Flying Mud Boat in 2010 to coincide with an exhibition.

From a distance, the architectural creation looks like it’s floating, but up close you can appreciate all the finer details, including the wire structure that holds it in place.

▼ On one side there are doors, which act as a small entrance into the structure.

The interior isn’t normally open to the public, but during special guided tours, a ladder is used so people can climb up to the boat and crawl inside.

▼ A beautiful spot for a teahouse.

As it turns out, the Flying Mud Boat isn’t the only unusual building in the area, as there are several other distinctive structures nearby, als0 designed by Fujimori.

One of these structures is a teahouse, cutely named Takasugian, which roughly translates as “Too-High Teahouse”.

▼ Nestled in amongst the treetops, this is another functioning teahouse in a dream setting.


This structure sits way above ground, perched atop two trees in such a whimsical manner that you’ll feel like you’ve stepped into the world of Studio Ghibli.


Ghibli’s animated feature movies are filled with architectural wonders that seem to defy all the rules, and this structure brings the same sort of anime wizardry to life in the real world. Despite the precarious look of it, the teahouse is structurally sound, but it’s located so high up that even looking at it from ground level is enough to make your heart skip a beat.

▼ Takasugi-an was once chosen by TIME magazine as one of the “Top 10 Most Dangerous Buildings in the World”, with the Leaning Tower of Pisa taking first place.

From a teahouse that’s too high comes one that’s too low, with the next structure being partly built underground.

Called Hikusugian , or “Too-Low Teahouse”, this is the complete opposite of Takasugian, literally sitting in its shadow.

Though none of the buildings were open when Natsuno visited, just seeing them was enough to spark a sense of awe inside of her. It also opened her eyes to what’s possible outside of traditional norms.

There’s also a community center designed by Fujimori in the vicinity, which puts his creative genius on full display.


From a teahouse that’s high up, to another down low, and then one suspended in the air – who knew teahouses could be so wonderfully unconventional? It’s a truly fascinating site that deserves to be more well-known, so next time you’re looking to enjoy some quiet time off the beaten path in Japan, be sure to put the Flying Mud Boat on your calendar.

title: Tiny no-screen digital camera gives us near-instant nostalgia by making us wait to see our pics
description: Kenko Tokina makes us think about our shots and feel extra emotion when we finally see how they turned out. content:
Kenko Tokina makes us think about our shots and feel extra emotion when we finally see how they turned out.

Recently, our Japanese-language reporter Go Hatori has gotten really into taking pictures, so much so that instead of using his phone for them, he wanted a dedicated device. After looking over his camera options, he decided to treat himself to the Pieni II from Kenko Tokina, a Japanese manufacturer primarily known as a lens maker.

There are a couple of reasons why Go chose this model, one of which is easy to see, and one of which, in a sense, is not easy to see. Let’s start with the easy one, though.

The Pieni II is incredibly compact. Though it’s a legitimate, functional photo-taking device, the packaging describes it as a “toy camera” because of how tiny it is.

Included with the camera is a strap so wear it around your neck, but the camera is so compact that you could even attach it to your key ring or use a clip, like the one Go picked up at a 100 yen store, to attach it to your bag or beltloop.

And as for the “not easy to see” reason Go chose this camera? Well, although this is a digital camera, with a slot to insert a microSD card on which to save your images…

…there’s no screen.

That means you don’t get a preview image, constantly being updated in real time, showing you the exact composition and lighting your image will have. Instead, you have a little clear viewfinder to help you see where the lens is pointed, and that’s it. What’s more, the Pieni II doesn’t have an app or any other sort of wireless connectivity that automatically uploads your photos to cloud storage or your other devices. In order to see how your photos turned out, you have to pop the SD card itself out of the camera and into your PC or phone.

In other words, the Pieni II’s design eliminates the instant results that are usually part of digital photography and replaces it with a gap in time between when you take a photo and when you see it, bringing back the exciting sense of anticipation from when film cameras were the norm. That’s the sensation that Go has been chasing as he takes photos, and he’s very, very happy with how some of his photos with his new camera have turned out.

Looking at the photos, you can probably guess the other thing Go loves about this camera. The Pieni II (which Go picked up for 5,280 yen [33] on Amazon Japan) isn’t designed for taking ultra-high-resolution images. In fact, its 1.31-megapixel count is pretty paltry by today’s standards.

On the other hand, that level of resolution is a great fit with the nostalgic retro-tech vibes of taking pictures without a preview screen.

The resolution isn’t so low that the photos become a blurry mess, but the softer lines and lower-key colors make then look like there were taken years ago, and add a sort of wistful significance to scenes of the present day.

All of a sudden, a quick selfie snapped with a friend feels like a precious memento that you’ve treasured for ages, and ordinary scenery looks like it could be a jazz fusion album cover.

Of course, the camera not having a screen means there’s no way to know right away when you’ve taken a dud that needs to be deleted, and when Go “develops” his photos by slotting the microSD card into his PC, he’ll always find at least a few that aren’t worth keeping.

That minor frustration, though, pales in comparison with the immense satisfaction he feels when one of his shots comes out just right and feels miraculously cool.
